intro.heading_en: The Devī’s Dialogue with the Messenger
intro.carita: Uttama Carita (the third episode, chapters 5–13), which begins here. In the recitation tradition its presiding form is Mahāsarasvatī, with Rudra as ṛṣi and anuṣṭubh as metre, and its dhyāna pictures her as born from the body of Gaurī (गौरीदेहसमुद्भवाम्) and as the slayer of Śumbha and the other daityas; this is the Gita Press viniyoga, not a statement of the Purāṇa text.
intro.summary: Medhas begins the third story (5.1). The asura brothers Śumbha and Niśumbha, trusting in pride and strength, seize from Indra the three worlds and the shares of the sacrifice (5.2), and take over the offices of the Sun, the Moon, Kubera, Yama, Varuṇa, Wind and Fire (5.3–4). The gods, defeated and driven out, remember the Unconquered Goddess and the boon she gave them: remembered in calamity, she would destroy their calamities at once (5.5–6). They go to the Himālaya and praise her as Viṣṇumāyā (5.7). Their hymn (5.9–82) opens with salutations to her names (5.9–13), runs through the yā devī stanzas, which find her in all beings as consciousness, intelligence, sleep, hunger, shadow, power, thirst and the rest, down to delusion (5.14–76), sums them up in a śloka on the all-pervading Goddess (5.77) and a last stanza on her as consciousness pervading the world (5.78–80), and closes, in a new metre, with a prayer that she bring good and strike down calamity (5.81–82). While they praise, Pārvatī comes to bathe in the Gaṅgā and asks whom they are praising; Śivā comes forth from the sheath of her body and answers that the hymn is hers (5.84–86). She is called Kauśikī, and Pārvatī, now dark, is called Kālikā and stays on the Himālaya (5.87–88). Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, Śumbha’s servants, see Ambikā’s beauty and report it to their master, listing every treasure he has already taken from the gods and asking why he does not take this ‘jewel among women’ too (5.89–100). Śumbha sends the asura Sugrīva as envoy (5.102–104). The envoy boasts of his master’s power and offers her either brother as husband (5.106–114). Grave, but smiling within, the Devī agrees that all he says is true, but she has a vow: whoever conquers her in battle, humbles her pride and matches her strength shall be her husband (5.116–121). The envoy calls her proud and threatens that she will be dragged by the hair (5.123–126); she repeats that her vow was made long ago and sends him back to tell Śumbha (5.128–129).
intro.forms: Aparājitā, the Unconquered, remembered by the conquered gods (5.5); Viṣṇumāyā, the name with which the hymn begins and the yā devī series opens (5.7, 5.14–16); in the salutations, Devī, Mahādevī, Śivā, Prakṛti and Bhadrā (5.9), Raudrā, Nityā, Gaurī, Dhātrī and the Moon’s light (5.10), Kalyāṇī, Nairṛtī, the fortune of kings and Śarvāṇī (5.11), Durgā, Kṛṣṇā and Dhūmrā (5.12), the most gentle and most terrible at once (5.13); in the yā devī stanzas, the powers present in every being, from consciousness (5.17–19) to delusion (5.74–76); Vyāptidevī, presiding over the senses and the elements (5.77); citi, consciousness pervading the world (5.78–80); the Sovereign (Īśvarī, Īśā) of the closing prayer (5.81–82). In the narrative: Pārvatī (5.84), Śivā who comes forth from her (5.85), Ambikā called Kauśikī (5.87), Kālikā, Pārvatī turned dark (5.88), and, at the reply, Durgā, Bhagavatī, Bhadrā, by whom the world is upheld (5.116).
intro.significance: The chapter holds the most recited hymn of the whole text, the gods’ praise with its refrain नमस्तस्यै, and the turn from hymn to story is immediate: the Goddess the gods have just found in all beings steps out of Pārvatī’s body in answer to her own question. The rest of the chapter sets the terms of the third story. The asuras see her only as a treasure to add to their plunder; she answers their claim of possession with a vow of battle. Nothing is fought in this chapter, but the war of chapters 6–10 is already decided by its two speeches.
intro.grammar: The hymn is built on the dative of homage with नमः (देव्यै, शिवायै, and the -ai datives of i-stems: प्रकृत्यै, कृत्यै, 5.9, 5.13) and on the relative-correlative frame या … तस्यै with the instrumental of manner …रूपेण संस्थिता (5.20–76). The narrative has perfects in both voices of √कृ (चक्राते, चक्रतुः, 5.3–4), a genitive absolute (5.84) and a locative absolute (5.88), and taddhitas of belonging (ऐन्दवम्, कौबेरम्, याम्यम्, 5.3; कौशिकी, 5.87). The speeches use passive imperatives as polite commands (ज्ञायताम्, गृह्यताम्, 5.91; श्रूयताम्, 5.119), gerundives (वक्तव्या, कार्यम्, 5.103), the optative in rhetorical questions (तिष्ठेत्, 5.123), मा with the imperative and the future (5.123, 5.126), and some epic forms beside the classical ones (शृणुष्व, 5.107; प्राप्स्यसे, 5.114). The closing prayer leaves the anuṣṭubh for vaṃśastha and indravaṃśā (5.81–82).
intro.teaching: Literally, dispossessed gods sing a hymn, a goddess comes out of Pārvatī, and two demons hear of her beauty and send a messenger to claim her, who is refused with a vow. As teaching, the hymn says that the Goddess is not found only in what is noble: intelligence and faith, but also sleep, hunger, thirst and error, are named as her forms in every being (5.20–76), and all of them are states of one consciousness (5.78–80). The story then shows what it is to miss this: the asuras, who own every treasure of the three worlds, can see her only as one more treasure (5.100, 5.112), and offer her a sovereignty that is already hers (5.114, 5.116). Her answer, that only one who conquers her may have her, is read in the Śākta tradition as a statement that she is not possessed.
themes: Remembrance (smṛti) and the promise of help
The Goddess in all beings: the yā devī hymn
Kauśikī: the Goddess who comes from Pārvatī’s body
Possession and its blindness: the logic of jewels
The vow: sovereignty that cannot be owned

conclusion.narrative: Robbed of their offices by Śumbha and Niśumbha, the gods do the one thing left to them: they remember the Goddess’s promise and praise her on the Himālaya, finding her in every state of every being. Their hymn is answered at once, when Śivā steps out of Pārvatī’s body, is named Kauśikī, and leaves Pārvatī dark as Kālikā. The asuras learn of her only through her beauty, and the chapter ends in an exchange of words: an offer of marriage made from the pride of possession, and a vow of battle that the Devī calls foolish but cannot break (5.128–129).

vocabulary.en: Viṣṇu’s Māyā: the Goddess as the power named in all beings
remembered: the condition on which she comes to help
power, capacity; the Goddess as power
office, a god’s function in the cosmos
share of the sacrifice, the gods’ portion
she who came from the sheath (कोश) of Pārvatī’s body
jewel; the best of any kind (elephant, horse, woman)

constructions: The dative of homage with नमः, and the -ai dative of feminine i-stems (प्रकृत्यै, कृत्यै, 5.9, 5.13).
The yā devī frame: relative या with correlative तस्यै, the instrumental of manner …रूपेण and the participle संस्थिता (5.20–76).
Perfects of √कृ in both voices for the same subjects (चक्राते, 5.3; चक्रतुः, 5.4).
Absolute constructions: genitive (स्तवादियुक्तानां देवानाम्, 5.84) and locative (तस्यां विनिर्गतायाम्, 5.88).
The passive imperative as a polite command (ज्ञायताम्, गृह्यताम्, 5.91; श्रूयताम्, 5.119).
The gerundive with the person told as subject (वक्तव्या, 5.103) and impersonal कार्यम् with the agent त्वया.
The general relative clause with present for future, closed by a future main verb (यो मां जयति … स मे भर्ता भविष्यति, 5.120).
Prohibition and warning with मा: मा … ब्रूहि (5.123), मा गमिष्यसि ‘lest you go’ (5.126).
insights: Remembrance is the gods’ only weapon, and it is enough: her promise was given for the moment of remembering (5.6), and the hymn ends by restating it as a fact about her (5.82).
No condition of a being is outside the Goddess: hunger, thirst and error are named beside intelligence, faith and peace (5.26–28, 5.35–37, 5.74–76).
All her forms are forms of one consciousness, which pervades the whole world (5.17–19, 5.78–80).
The Goddess who is praised and the Goddess who asks are one: Śivā answers from within Pārvatī (5.85–86).
Those who own everything cannot see her except as one more possession (5.100, 5.112); what they offer her is already hers (5.114, 5.116).
She is won by no one: her only ‘husband’ would be one who conquers her and is her equal in strength (5.120).
conclusion.srividya: The hymn shares many names with the Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa): Viṣṇumāyā (339, विष्णुमाया), Mahādevī (209, महादेवी), Śivā (53, शिवा), Durgā (190, दुर्गा), Kalyāṇī (324, कल्याणी), Śarvāṇī (124, शर्वाणी), Gaurī (635, गौरी), and several of the qualities of the yā devī stanzas, among them तुष्टिः (443), शान्तिः (447), कान्तिः (449), स्मृतिः (540) and लज्जा (740); the idea of the Goddess as consciousness is shared too (362, चितिः; 417, चेतनारूपा). In the narrative Pārvatī (246, पार्वती) and Ambikā (295, अम्बिका) are names of both texts. These are shared Śākta names and ideas, not evidence that one text depends on the other; the story of Kauśikī’s emergence belongs to the Devī Māhātmya, and no specifically Śrīvidyā doctrine is stated in this chapter.

key_verses.why: The boon recalled: remembered in calamity, she will destroy the gods’ gravest calamities at that very instant.
नमो देव्यै महादेव्यै — the opening of the gods’ hymn.
The first yā devī stanza: homage to the Goddess who in all beings is named Viṣṇumāyā.
The last stanza of the series: she who, as consciousness, pervades this whole world and abides in it.
Ambikā comes forth from the sheath of Pārvatī’s body and is celebrated in all the worlds as Kauśikī.
Grave yet smiling within, Durgā, by whom this world is upheld, answers Śumbha’s envoy.
The vow: whoever conquers her in battle, humbles her pride and is her equal in strength shall be her husband.

sandhi_patterns: Visarga sandhi is by far the commonest junction: -aḥ before voiced sounds → -o (नमो देव्यै), visarga → s/ś before t/c (नमस्तस्यै, निशुम्भश्चातिवीर्यवान्), and -aḥ + a → -o’ (दूतोऽहं, 5.106; शुम्भोऽत्र, 5.121).
सः and एषः drop the visarga before any consonant (स तत्र, 5.104; स मे, 5.120; एष महापद्मः, 5.96).

Savarṇa-dīrgha, with the Gita Press double avagraha marking a long ā (यथाऽऽपत्सु, 5.6; पुराऽऽसीत्, 5.97); yaṇ (संस्मरन्त्यपराजिताम्, 5.5; देव्युवाच); vṛddhi (तथैन्दवम्, 5.3; मैवं, 5.123); pūrvarūpa (स्तूयतेऽत्र, 5.85; तेऽङ्गणे, 5.95).
Final m → anusvāra before consonants throughout; t → n before a nasal (कस्मान्न, 5.100; वचनान्मम, 5.103); ch doubled after a short vowel (सर्वभूतेषुच्छाया-, 5.29–31).
One declared hiatus: आख्याता | अतीव at the pāda break of 5.90, where the reported speech begins.
samasa: Ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣas throughout the narrative (शचीपतिः, यज्ञभागाः, शरीरकोशः), several of them ‘of selection’ (स्त्रीरत्नम्, गजरत्नम्).
In the yā devī stanzas, karmadhārayas whose first member is the form itself (बुद्धिरूपेण, निद्रारूपेण …, ‘the form that is intelligence’).
Bahuvrīhis of epithet, including feminines in -ī from body-parts (चञ्चलापाङ्गी, 5.113; अतिचार्वङ्गी, 5.92) and nested ones (केशाकर्षणनिर्धूतगौरवा, 5.126).
Upapada tatpuruṣas with agent forms (सर्वकारिणी, 5.12; रत्नभुजः, 5.112; पुरन्दरः, 5.94), and dvandvas of the paired brothers (शुम्भनिशुम्भयोः).
grammar_notes: स्म in 5.9 is printed short for the metre; read as the particle with the copula understood, or as स्मः with the visarga lost metri causa — the sense is the same.
प्रणताम् (5.11) is taken as a short genitive plural ‘of those who bow’; its derivation is uncertain.
The two voices of √कृ stand side by side for the same subjects (चक्राते, 5.3; चक्रतुः, 5.4).
In 5.104 the kept Gita Press reading makes सा देवी the subject of यत्रास्ते; the GRETIL and Freund reading is smoother.
Several epic or ārṣa forms are kept as printed: शृणुष्व (5.107), प्राप्स्यसे (5.114), parasmaipada व्यपोहति (5.120), मा with the imperative (5.123).
The closing prayer changes metre: vaṃśastha (5.81) and indravaṃśā (5.82) after the anuṣṭubh of the hymn.
themes: Remembrance and the promise of help
Kauśikī and Kālikā: the emergence from Pārvatī
uncertain: 5.11: नैर्ऋत्यै (Gita Press) / नैरृत्यै (GRETIL, Freund) — orthographic only.
5.104: सा देवी तां ततः प्राह (Gita Press) / तां च देवीं ततः प्राह (GRETIL, Freund) — Textual Verification Required.
5.128: निशुम्भश्चातिवीर्यवान् (Gita Press) / निशुम्भश्चापि तादृशः (GRETIL, Freund) — Textual Verification Required.
Interpretive doubts are flagged on 5.9, 5.11, 5.41–43, 5.59–61, 5.77 and 5.82.
